items.title: Frida 17.24.2 Released
items.summary: A Darwin fix release, all of it by @hsorbo , centered on thread-locals in images mapped by our out-of-process mapper, which lets us inject the agent on macOS and iOS without relying on dlopen() in the target, where a sandbox may not allow it. Thread-locals in mapped images Our Darwin mapper only provisioned thread-local storage for the thread that ran the constructors, and pointed every TLV descriptor at dyld’s tlv_get_addr . Any other thread then went through dyld’s slow path, which knows nothing about an image it didn’t load, and got zero-filled storage of an unknown size. With the V8 runtime that crashed on its JS thread, and on macOS 26 the __dyld_apis layout also made tlv_get_addr read as NULL . The descriptors now point at our own thunk, for arm64 and x86-64. On first use from a thread it allocates the block, copies in the __thread_data template and stores it through pthread_setspecific() , so libpthread frees it when the thread exits. Like dyld’s, it clobbers nothing but the result register, so compiled code may keep live values, vector registers included, across a thread-local access. On unload, the calling thread’s block is freed before the key is deleted, as pthread_key_delete() clears the slot in every thread without running the destructor. Along the way, the TLV runtime stopped calling pthread_key_create() and pthread_key_delete() through pointers signed in our own process. Such pointers only authenticate in the target if it shares our PAC keys, which it does not when the two are signed by different teams. They are now called without authentication, like the injector does, and the thunk is signed in the target, since the descriptors are IA auth binds that compiled code calls through blraaz . Arm64Writer gained PACIZA for that, as PACIA treats register 31 as SP rather than XZR . All of it is covered by a new test that maps a small dylib with thread-locals and checks the lifecycle from fresh per-thread storage to unload. Helper The macOS helper inherited the parent’s end of the control socket, so it held both ends of the pair. The parent’s end is now close-on-exec, with a test that spawns a process and checks the helper’s descriptors. Enjoy! Changelog darwin-mapper: Allocate TLV storage per thread through our own thunk, on arm64 and x86-64, fixing V8 crashes on its JS thread and NULL tlv_get_addr on macOS 26. Thanks @hsorbo ! darwin-mapper: Free the calling thread’s TLV block on unload. Thanks @hsorbo ! darwin-mapper: Call the pthread key functions without authentication, and sign the TLV thunk in the target, so it works when the target is signed by another team. Thanks @hsorbo ! arm64-writer: Add PACIZA . Thanks @hsorbo ! darwin: Don’t leak the control socket to the helper. Thanks @hsorbo !
items.summary_html:
A Darwin fix release, all of it by @hsorbo, centered on thread-locals in images mapped by our out-of-process mapper, which lets us inject the agent on macOS and iOS without relying on dlopen() in the target, where a sandbox may not allow it.

Thread-locals in mapped images

Our Darwin mapper only provisioned thread-local storage for the thread that ran the constructors, and pointed every TLV descriptor at dyld’s tlv_get_addr. Any other thread then went through dyld’s slow path, which knows nothing about an image it didn’t load, and got zero-filled storage of an unknown size. With the V8 runtime that crashed on its JS thread, and on macOS 26 the __dyld_apis layout also made tlv_get_addr read as NULL.

The descriptors now point at our own thunk, for arm64 and x86-64. On first use from a thread it allocates the block, copies in the __thread_data template and stores it through pthread_setspecific(), so libpthread frees it when the thread exits. Like dyld’s, it clobbers nothing but the result register, so compiled code may keep live values, vector registers included, across a thread-local access. On unload, the calling thread’s block is freed before the key is deleted, as pthread_key_delete() clears the slot in every thread without running the destructor.

Along the way, the TLV runtime stopped calling pthread_key_create() and pthread_key_delete() through pointers signed in our own process. Such pointers only authenticate in the target if it shares our PAC keys, which it does not when the two are signed by different teams. They are now called without authentication, like the injector does, and the thunk is signed in the target, since the descriptors are IA auth binds that compiled code calls through blraaz. Arm64Writer gained PACIZA for that, as PACIA treats register 31 as SP rather than XZR. All of it is covered by a new test that maps a small dylib with thread-locals and checks the lifecycle from fresh per-thread storage to unload.

Helper

The macOS helper inherited the parent’s end of the control socket, so it held both ends of the pair. The parent’s end is now close-on-exec, with a test that spawns a process and checks the helper’s descriptors.

Enjoy!

Changelog
  • darwin-mapper: Allocate TLV storage per thread through our own thunk, on arm64 and x86-64, fixing V8 crashes on its JS thread and NULL tlv_get_addr on macOS 26. Thanks @hsorbo!
  • darwin-mapper: Free the calling thread’s TLV block on unload. Thanks @hsorbo!
  • darwin-mapper: Call the pthread key functions without authentication, and sign the TLV thunk in the target, so it works when the target is signed by another team. Thanks @hsorbo!
  • arm64-writer: Add PACIZA. Thanks @hsorbo!
  • darwin: Don’t leak the control socket to the helper. Thanks @hsorbo!

items.title: OpenCode Security Breach Exposes Third-Party API Keys of its Console Users
items.summary: OpenCode has disclosed a security breach affecting 1.4% of its Console users, warning that third-party API keys saved in affected workspaces may have been exposed. In an October 17 statement, the company linked the incident to a large-scale distillation attack and said it was working with Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google to address it. The affected group was limited to some Console users who had linked external providers. OpenCode said it had emailed everyone affected that morning and stated that users who did not receive an email were not impacted. The percentage refers to Console users, not the entire OpenCode user base. Legacy System Access Put Provider Keys at Risk A notification shared in the supplied screenshot says OpenCode identified unauthorized access to a legacy system that it was already preparing to shut down. Third-party provider keys stored in users’ workspaces, including those for OpenAI and Anthropic, may have been exposed. The notice asks recipients to revoke and replace those keys through each provider’s dashboard, update applications that use them, and review recent usage for unexpected activity. Its wording describes possible exposure rather than confirming that every affected key was stolen or used. OpenCode’s public statement does not explain how attackers gained access, how long they remained inside, or how many keys were involved. It also does not name an attacker or provide technical evidence showing how the breach supported the reported distillation activity. Distillation involves training one AI model using responses generated by another. In an unauthorized campaign, attackers can collect large amounts of model output without permission. Cybersecurity News previously covered Anthropic’s warnings about large scale distillation attacks , explaining how repeated requests can help transfer capabilities between models. However, OpenCode has not explained whether exposed credentials were used to make those requests. Its statement establishes a reported connection, not a complete account of the attack. There is also no confirmed loss figure in the public disclosure. The wider risk of exposed credentials has appeared in earlier reporting on API keys found in public web data . That separate case illustrates why secret storage and removal matter, but it does not establish a shared attacker or method here. items.summary_html:
OpenCode has disclosed a security breach affecting 1.4% of its Console users, warning that third-party API keys saved in affected workspaces may have been exposed. In an October 17 statement, the company linked the incident to a large-scale distillation attack and said it was working with Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google to address it.

The affected group was limited to some Console users who had linked external providers. OpenCode said it had emailed everyone affected that morning and stated that users who did not receive an email were not impacted. The percentage refers to Console users, not the entire OpenCode user base.

Legacy System Access Put Provider Keys at Risk

A notification shared in the supplied screenshot says OpenCode identified unauthorized access to a legacy system that it was already preparing to shut down. Third-party provider keys stored in users’ workspaces, including those for OpenAI and Anthropic, may have been exposed.

The notice asks recipients to revoke and replace those keys through each provider’s dashboard, update applications that use them, and review recent usage for unexpected activity. Its wording describes possible exposure rather than confirming that every affected key was stolen or used.

OpenCode’s public statement does not explain how attackers gained access, how long they remained inside, or how many keys were involved. It also does not name an attacker or provide technical evidence showing how the breach supported the reported distillation activity.

Distillation involves training one AI model using responses generated by another. In an unauthorized campaign, attackers can collect large amounts of model output without permission. Cybersecurity News previously covered Anthropic’s warnings about large scale distillation attacks, explaining how repeated requests can help transfer capabilities between models.

However, OpenCode has not explained whether exposed credentials were used to make those requests. Its statement establishes a reported connection, not a complete account of the attack. There is also no confirmed loss figure in the public disclosure.

The wider risk of exposed credentials has appeared in earlier reporting on API keys found in public web data. That separate case illustrates why secret storage and removal matter, but it does not establish a shared attacker or method here.

Affected Users Urged to Replace Keys

For notified users, the immediate response is the key replacement process described in the warning. Reviewing provider usage alongside recent billing records can help identify requests that need investigation. Replacing a key also requires updating every application that depends on it.

OpenCode said the incident remained ongoing when it published its statement and that it could not share more details. A fuller technical report would help establish the entry point, the scope of credential exposure, and whether unauthorized model requests occurred.
